summary: Very noisy aircraft flying over a housing estate.
description: On the evening of December 2, 1985, around 10:00 PM, several witnesses heard a loud, muffled noise. Going outside, they saw a cluster of lights on a flying object: red lights at the front and rear, and bright lights in the middle. The object moved slowly over the housing development, and the lights and the craft gradually disappeared. The investigation suggests the possibility of a Transall aircraft, scheduled to fly over the town that evening at that time.

summary: Likely observation of an advertising spotlight beam
description: On November 16, 1985, a witness observed a circular display of five white discs from his fourth-floor apartment. This display appeared to occur approximately 2 km away and within a 500-meter radius. The discs formed a square around a central disc. Then, the four discs moved towards the central disc, which grew larger and brighter. The initial pattern suddenly resumed and then abruptly disappeared. No sound was heard. Although this hypothesis was not investigated further by the police, the witness's description leads us to favor the hypothesis of a display of "sky rose" type laser beams.

summary: Phenomenon evolving in the sky
description: On September 20, 1985, at approximately 7:15 a.m., two witnesses observed a bright, circular, stationary object in the sky that resembled a star. During this rather lengthy observation, one of the witnesses, equipped with binoculars, saw the object flatten into a cigar shape. From one end, a point of light appeared to detach and move slowly, leaving behind bright turbulence. Two to three minutes later, the phenomenon returned to its initial shape. Around 7:40 a.m., clouds completely obscured the phenomenon. No further information could be gathered about this event.

summary: Two large spotlights emitting a very powerful white light.
description: On October 8, 1985, witnesses observed unusual luminous phenomena. Despite the stormy weather and lightning present that early evening, one witness saw two beams of blinding light four times in succession: the light source appeared to be located 1 km from his home, above a group of trees arranged in a straight line. Two other witnesses saw red, blue, and white lights appear three times in succession. No further information could be gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Probable sighting of an aircraft.
description: On October 5, 1985, at approximately 7:20 PM, a motorist and his passengers observed a large luminous phenomenon. As this phenomenon moved, they saw a triangular shape with flashing green and red lights. No noise was heard, and the estimated speed was 80 to 100 km/h. The investigation revealed that 25-minute training flights had taken place over the same area with a Cessna 150 aircraft. The pilot, who repeatedly illuminated the cockpit and switched on the landing lights for his students, observed nothing unusual during these flights. It is likely that the witnesses saw the aircraft in question during one of the passes over the area.

summary: probable observation of an astronomical phenomenon.
description: Between September 16 and 18, 1985, several witnesses observed a bright, fixed point in the sky with faint red, blue, yellow, or green hues. These observations, which lasted for several days and sometimes two hours, were confirmed by staff at the Alpes de Haute-Provence Observatory. It was likely the observation of a planet or a star.

summary: Strange phenomenon at high altitude
description: On September 14, 1985, at 5:00 PM, a witness observed a dome-shaped object with lights inside for an hour. Much later that evening, using binoculars, the object appeared to be followed by an incandescent glow. The observation was also made with binoculars by the gendarmerie and the director of an observatory; unfortunately, fog prevented any observation with a telescope. No further information has been gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: A fixed, bright light in the shape of a boomerang.
description: On September 12, 1985, at approximately 6:45 PM, a witness observed a fixed, boomerang-shaped light. He observed this golden-yellow light through binoculars for almost an hour before it disappeared. No other witness statements or information have been gathered regarding this case.

summary: Observations of the silent passage of a luminous object in the sky; observation of a glow in a basin of the port E.Herriot in Lyon: probable observations of a meteorite reentry.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. This re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named Lyon (69) 1985, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On September 3, 1985, four witnesses in Lyon (2 witnesses) and also in Villefranche-sur-Saône (2 witnesses) were surprised by the rapid passage of a luminous phenomenon in the sky and, for some, by the presence of a peculiar glow in the water of a pool. The description of the UFO by the various witnesses is typical of a meteoroid reentry: - observation duration of a few seconds, high speed of movement, - glow and halo ("fluorescent green color (somewhat like Bengal lights), surrounded by a white veil", "a bright, pale green ball, surrounded by a dark green halo"), - temporal conjunction of almost identical observations by distant witnesses (here Villefranche-sur-Saône and Lyon), - indications of consistent trajectories. To confirm this hypothesis, it is necessary to explain some unusual elements of this reentry: - the meteorite falls into the water and glows from the water for a few minutes: there are 3 witnesses to the UFO in the sky (T2, a security guard in Lyon, T3 and T4 in Villefranche-sur-Saône). None of them saw it fall into the water, but for witness T2 from Lyon, there is a correlation between the observed trajectory of the UFO in the sky and the glow in the water observed by T2 and T1 (T1, a truck driver, did not see the UFO in the sky). It is reasonable to assume that the meteorite did indeed fall into the water. We should not attach any importance to T1 and T2's estimate of the size of the glow in the water as "30 m" (such a large meteorite would have caused a tidal wave!) because this estimate refers to the glow rising to the surface of the water and cannot be applied to the source of the glow. Witness T1 also said, "I saw a fairly large glow, yellowish-white in color, a bit like a diver shining a light from inside the water," while T2 estimated the size of the source of the glow to be the size of a football. - Firefighters detected slight radioactivity, described as "minimal," both in and out of the water: this finding did not lead to further investigation. In the absence of any record of the area where this low level of radioactivity was present over time and space, it is difficult to definitively confirm that it was caused by the meteorite. Even if it were, this would not rule out the meteorite hypothesis. - T1 noted this unusual phenomenon: the security vehicle's indicator light was flashing. The police report states that this was seen by three witnesses (T1, T2, and another security officer, a colleague of T2, mentioned in the report but who did not give a statement) for four seconds at the moment of the impact. However, this was only formally reported (police statement) by T1 (T2, who was using the vehicle, makes no mention of it in his statement), and T1 observed it upon arriving at the scene after the fall and does not specify having seen the beginning and end of this flashing. It is common that in a situation of alert or emotion, a secondary anomaly is detected or even associated with another primary anomaly, whereas without the latter and the tension created, it might have gone unnoticed or been put into perspective (here, the witness, who is not a security officer but a truck driver, was indeed on high alert because he was sent by the security manager to the scene where the security officers were already reporting something unidentified by radio; T1 also says that he took the wrong route to get there). Consequently, with conformity to a meteorite reentry being proven and the singular elements of the testimonies explained, GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable meteoroid reentry.

summary: Object of spherical shape.
description: On September 13, 1985, around 3:00 PM, several witnesses, including police officers, observed a bright white mass moving silently along the marked trail leading to the volcano for a few minutes. This boomerang-shaped object exhibited oscillatory movements: it suddenly gained altitude and took on a spherical shape before disappearing without a trace. Following a press article on the subject, another person came forward to report the same sighting on August 6, 1985, a few kilometers away. No further information has emerged to confirm either of the local police's hypotheses.

summary: Object in the shape of a "delta".
description: On August 1, 1985, at approximately 11:15 PM, a witness observed a fixed, luminous, slightly reddish point in the sky, resembling a star. This point then moved vertically above the village, changing color and brightness to take on a delta shape and moving horizontally at an increasing speed. The witness noted that a few seconds after its vertical movement, a muffled sound was heard, and that as it moved away, the object reverted to a point of light. No other observations of this phenomenon have been recorded.

summary: luminous phenomenon in the night sky observed for a long time and from several places; no noise and sudden disappearance: confusion with a set of spotlights whose beams impacted the lower cloud layer.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named PLOERMEL (56) 1985, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined (see the investigation report). On the night of July 22-23, 1985, at 11:15 PM, a witness observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon from their home. Until 3:30 a.m., the witness and others observed the phenomenon from various locations in the Ploërmel area (56). The phenomenon was described as oval-shaped, emitting a thin white light accompanied by a luminous source rotating around it. The witness described a luminous phenomenon that seemed to sweep across the sky from side to side. No sound was heard. The phenomenon disappeared suddenly. Only one witness account was collected. This observation, which at first glance seems extraordinary, appears to be the spatial and temporal coincidence of a particular unusual phenomenon occurring in an equally unusual context. Two hypotheses were explored and are ultimately quite similar, as they both involve the observation of beams of light from spotlights impacting a low cloud layer: - beams from a night vision device (Skytracer); - beams from the Saint-Cyr triumph at the Coëtquidan military camp. Although some discrepancies exist, particularly regarding the directions of the UFO for the observation phases carried out from the Gendarmerie barracks, numerous points of agreement can be found between these hypotheses and the physical and dynamic characteristics of the UFO, as well as with the observation conditions: - overall observation direction towards the east (except from point D for the skytrackers hypothesis); - visibility as provided by Météo-France data consistent with the observation distances; - presence of a low cloud layer; - observation low on the horizon possible because the horizons were clear from at least two observation points and consistent with the distances considered and the cloud altitude; - main shape of the UFO ovoid; - presence of beams of light; - proven movement of the UFO, like a set of moving spotlights; - low brightness; - white color; Other aspects of the phenomenon fit poorly or less well with one or both hypotheses. We will focus in particular on: - the rectangular shape observed to the left of the main shape in phases 2, 3, and 5; - the UFO's position in phase 4, too far north as deduced from the reproduction in Bretagne-Magazine, near the observation site. Is this reproduction (outside the GEIPAN survey area) accurate? (If it had included houses in the landscape, the conclusion regarding the observation direction would have been consistent). Is this a different phenomenon? - the use of spotlights for the unlikely nightclub hypothesis; The Monday evening date would imply that the nightclub was open outside of the weekend, which is not out of the question during the summer months. Furthermore, regarding the "triumph" at Coëtquidan, which takes place on the night of a Saturday to Sunday following July 14th, it suggests that the event, or at least the spotlights, were being tested or adjusted. However, most of these points remain weak compared to the numerous and consistent aspects that make the hypotheses plausible, with the possibility of the spotlights being used during the "triumph" at the Coëtquidan military camp being particularly strong. Indeed, their existence is confirmed, and they could have been used a few days before (or after) the "triumph" ceremony to prepare for (or replay) any anomalies encountered during) the event. Such a hypothesis cannot be verified 33 years later, but nothing allows us to exclude it or consider it unlikely. Consequently, an eBe classification is appropriate: confusion with a set of spotlights where the impact of the beams is projected onto the lower cloud layer.

summary: Recent testimony of an old observation of the slow and low-altitude passage of a craft with two individuals: lack of information.
description: Recent testimony (March 2015) of an earlier sighting (July 1985). On July 22, 1985, at approximately 2:30 PM, a motorist and his passengers were surprised to see the front fuselage of a craft appear at a very low altitude and very slowly, followed by two individuals behind a window. The motorist stopped his vehicle and leaned over to get a closer look, but everything had disappeared. No other witness statements were collected. This very strange sighting report from 1985, describing unknown beings, was only submitted to GEIPAN in March 2015, nearly 30 years after the event. As with all cases of this kind, GEIPAN submitted the sighting account to a university cognitive psychology laboratory to assess the potential for false memories. The laboratory's report is attached. It appears that the strangest elements of the testimony are suspected of being false memories; nevertheless, the witness certainly saw an unusual flying object (a large solar balloon or a low-flying aircraft). Due to this testimony being distorted by false memories, and the lack of corroborating evidence, GEIPAN classifies this case as "C" due to a lack of reliable information.

summary: Object shaped like an upside-down plate changing direction.
description: On July 20, 1985, a witness reported seeing, along with others, a peculiar luminous phenomenon above a group of trees. Around 10:45 PM, in a clear, starry sky, a shape resembling an inverted plate topped with a dome emitted a white and yellow light. This stationary object gradually disappeared once, only to reappear again. No noise was heard during the observation, which lasted 40 minutes. The witness first alerted a radio station the following day, which then relayed the information to the local press. The police investigation failed to confirm the young girl's account on several points: one of the cited witnesses was not present, and the other did not corroborate the story. Furthermore, the weather conditions at the time did not correspond to those described by the witness. It seems that this testimony is not very credible and is likely the product of a teenage girl's fabrication.

summary: circular luminous phenomenon
description: On June 26, 1985, a witness observed a circular object, 1.5 meters in diameter and approximately 1.8 meters high, for five minutes. According to the witness, the object appeared to be composed of an unstable, gaseous substance. It hovered 5 meters above the ground and made no sound. An incandescent glow emanated from the object, which then suddenly dematerialized. The witness had previously made a similar observation in 1976. No further information has been gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: A bright point moving at high speed.
description: On June 5, 1985, at approximately 10:50 PM, a witness on his doorstep observed a bright white point of light for 10 seconds. This point moved across the sky at very rapid speed, silently, and in a zigzag pattern. No further information could be gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Observations of several luminous phenomena in the night sky during several observation phases: observations of thunderstorm lightning (phase 1) and lack of information for the rest of the observations.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named LA TRINITE PORHOUET (56) 1985, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On the night of May 25-26, 1985, between 11:00 PM and 1:30 AM, four witnesses observed various luminous phenomena. First (phase 1), the witnesses in a vehicle were intrigued by numerous flashes of light of different colors in the sky from various points along their route. Then, back at the family property (phase 2), the witnesses, scanning the starry sky, noticed two luminous points moving at an equal distance from each other at varying speeds. These points then disappeared, hidden by the landscape. It was then (phase 3) that, through a gap in the trees, they saw a luminous, red, rectangular object on the top of a hill. Frightened, the witnesses went back inside the house and conferred, unable to understand what they had seen. Finally, they heard a muffled noise (phase 4) and noticed a total silence in the countryside, which worried them. Going back outside a few minutes later, they saw nothing. The witnesses went to the Gendarmerie the next day. No other group of witnesses to these nocturnal phenomena was found among the local population. A four-phase observation sequence was noted, each phase leading to different descriptions of UFOs (see the investigation report). The starting point (phase 1) likely originated from thunderstorm lightning (recorded by the weather service in the west that evening), which the witnesses were unable to definitively identify (although this hypothesis was put forward) for several reasons: the witnesses were unfamiliar with the area, the lightning was very distant while the local sky was clear and storm-free, and the distance prevented them from hearing thunder. The following three phases were described in fleeting, imprecise, or contradictory terms, making it impossible to establish a sufficiently plausible explanation. Nevertheless, none of these observations seems strange, as there is at least one explanation for each that the limited information available can neither confirm nor refute: - the description of the UFOs in phase 2 is reminiscent of the lights of a simple aircraft, which, under certain observation conditions and depending on the type of lights present and illuminated, can take on a somewhat particular appearance; - the description of the UFO in phase 3 could correspond to a blood moon breaking through the clouds; - the description of the noise in phase 4 (no visual observation, as the witnesses were inside) could correspond to a rumble of thunder. The entire observation may have seemed strange at the time due to its apparently complex nature, and this strangeness is compounded by what the witnesses perceived. The experience accumulated since then at GEIPAN leads us to consider a phenomenon of amorage. The witnesses' initial observation may have placed them in a state of strangeness (likely amplified collectively, as none of them seemed able to moderate their accounts by developing the initial hypothesis of lightning during a thunderstorm), leading them to subsequently scrutinize the sky and associate this initial strangeness with other phenomena that might have gone unnoticed without it. The fact is that the police conducted inquiries among the villagers and the farming community to corroborate these testimonies and found nothing, even though that Saturday evening coincided with the village fair in Josselin (56) and was therefore conducive (and not only for the witnesses) to numerous late-night outings, including on the roads used by the witnesses. The consistency of the observation is poor. The data collected is too imprecise, even contradictory, when it is not entirely absent. For example, essential elements are missing, such as angular measurements, certain initial and final observation directions, observation durations, etc. However, the available data allows us to establish: - that the initial observation was probably caused by lightning from a thunderstorm; - and that the other observations are not very strange, probably would not have occurred without the persistent strangeness created by the initial observation, and cannot be explained due to a lack of reliable information. Consequently, GEIPAN concludes with category B (thunderstorm lightning) for the UFO of phase 1 and category C for the remaining observations.

summary: Observation of a large, red-colored object.
description: On April 8, 1985, several witnesses spotted an irregularly shaped, vermilion-red, ogive-shaped object falling straight down behind a mountain. Fearing it might be an aircraft in distress, the gendarmerie was immediately informed of the sighting and was also able to confirm the phenomenon. The investigation revealed it to be an expired marine distress flare launched without any particular intent by a resident of a nearby hamlet.

summary: probable observation of an astronomical phenomenon.
description: Starting on March 8, 1985, and for several days afterward, a witness observed a glow from the window of his 14th-floor apartment. This glow, "like a star," moved slowly. On March 18, 1985, while filming the glow, it suddenly appeared to move toward him. Frightened, he took refuge with neighbors. After investigation, it appears the witness saw Jupiter, which was particularly visible at that time of year.

summary: observation of an astronomical phenomenon.
description: Twice during March 1985, a witness observed a particularly bright point of light that moved very slowly but steadily across the sky. The investigation revealed that it was the planet Venus, which was particularly bright and therefore visible at that time of year.

summary: Flame-colored ball moving at an altitude of approximately 800 meters, following the terrain.
description: On March 2, 1985, at approximately 10:00 PM, a witness and his entire family observed a flame-colored sphere, about one meter in diameter, for 15 minutes. The object left trails of the same color in its wake. It moved slowly at an altitude of approximately 800 meters, following the contours of the land. No noise was heard. No further information about this phenomenon has been gathered.

summary: Fall of an object preceded by a whistling sound: fall of part of a German war machine (land-to-land machine "fog launcher") which spontaneously started to burn.
description: On February 25, 1985, two farmers were working in their fields when an object fell within 50 meters of one of them, bouncing several times before coming to rest. The object was brittle and could not be touched for at least an hour. It was a cylinder approximately 50 cm long and 15 cm in diameter. Initial investigations conducted by the Rochefort air base failed to identify the object, which did not correspond to any type of French or foreign missile. Furthermore, no radioactivity was detected on the recovered object. GEPAN (the French National Center for Astronomical Studies) also conducted a search, but no military activity could explain the fall of such an object. The investigation then focused on space objects that might have re-entered the atmosphere that day. Responses from NASA and NORAD indicate that a piece of the propulsion stage of the COSMOS 1629 satellite, launched on February 21 (reference 15.575), likely re-entered the atmosphere around the 25th. This information led GEPAN to the preliminary conclusion that a piece of the fourth stage of the COSMOS 1629 launch had re-entered the atmosphere. The object was, however, handed over to GEPAN by the airbase for further in-depth analysis. These in-depth analyses were later launched and carried out by the Arcueil Research and Study Center, which revealed indications and markings proving that the object was of German origin and bore the markings of the Third Reich. GEPAN's initial conclusion was therefore abandoned in favor of the hypothesis of a propulsion element of unknown origin, abandoned since the Second World War, which spontaneously ignited. Further expert analysis has allowed investigators to identify the device as the rear section of a land-based "fog launcher" and to determine that the point of origin of this device, which may have been ignited by thermal effect or a slight impact, can be estimated to be between 3,300 and 3,600 meters northwest of the impact site. This location corresponds to a marshy area where the German army, at the end of World War II, submerged numerous munitions while encircled in the Royan pocket. This investigation, which spanned nearly five years, is a model of its kind due to its evolution and successive developments.

summary: A red ball falls.
description: On February 24, 1985, at approximately 7:30 PM, several witnesses in the same area saw a pinkish-red sphere fall; an explosion was also heard. The investigation revealed that this was the effect of a distress flare launched unintentionally by someone, as the witnesses saw the pinkish-red smoke from the flare and then the parachute drifting with the wind.

summary: probable observation of a star.
description: On February 21, 1985, around 10 p.m., two witnesses observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon: a very bright yellow ball that changed color to bright red. For 20 minutes, the witnesses observed a stationary and silent phenomenon that gradually disappeared. The main witness, as well as several other people, also made this observation on subsequent nights. It was probably the sighting of a star that was particularly visible in the clear winter night sky.

summary: Large star mistaken for the planet Venus.
description: On February 17, 1985, at approximately 9:30 PM, several witnesses observed a very large star. This very bright star gradually changed color and quickly disappeared over the horizon. It was, in fact, the observation of the planet Venus, particularly visible at that time of year in Greece under specific weather conditions.

summary: Unidentified object appearing as a star with white and yellow luminosity.
description: On February 14, 1985, around 10 p.m., a witness, alone in his third-floor apartment, saw a peculiar white and yellow star. Suddenly, a green sphere appeared alongside the star. This phenomenon disappeared over the horizon without making a sound. No further information has been gathered about this event.

summary: A sphere emitting a bright light, twenty times brighter than that of a star.
description: On February 13th and 18th, 1985, several witnesses observed a silent luminous phenomenon in the sky at 9:30 PM: a sphere much larger than a star was moving slowly at a low altitude. Circular in shape and very bright white, this sphere disappeared very quickly from the field of vision of the witnesses, who nevertheless took the time to film the phenomenon. The hypothesis concerning the observation of a planet or a star could not be confirmed due to a lack of information gathered.

summary: Multiple observations of unusual phenomena moving in the sky on February 2nd and 4th, 1985: observations of February 2nd: observations of the star Arcturus. Observations of February 4th: probable observation of an airplane.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. Among its publications are older cases, originally classified as type D, which are now being re-examined solely to improve the relevance of the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired over the past few years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This observation, formerly known as ALDUDES (64) 1985, is one of the cases classified as type D by GEIPAN and has recently been re-examined. It actually consists of two completely different observations: one from February 2nd and the other from February 4th (see the investigation reports). The UFO of February 2nd corresponds to an observation of the star Arcturus. - This star, seen on the horizon, regularly creates misinterpretations due to its scintillation, bursts of color, and apparent movement: effects generated by the passage of light rays through the atmosphere. - There is perfect correspondence in azimuth directions. - The observation is accompanied by a rarer phenomenon of atmospheric refraction (superior mirage), which explains why the star is seen from beyond the horizon. This phenomenon also accentuates the classic misinterpretations linked to the passage of light through the atmosphere. It is not possible, 32 years later, to quantitatively confirm this atmospheric refraction. - The same observation is reported in the press (a group of night skiers in the Somport resort, see report). The repetition, two nights in a row, of a nearly identical UFO sighting by two independent groups of witnesses, with the same coincidence (within 1 or 2 degrees) in azimuth with Arcturus, and with the same type of observation beyond the horizon, validates the Arcturus hypothesis and the particular phenomenon of atmospheric refraction accompanying it. GEIPAN classifies this case as A: Arcturus sighting. The UFO of February 4th probably corresponds to an aircraft sighting. - The hypothesis was rejected by the witnesses due to the absence of noise from the UFO. The wind blowing from the Northwest acts in the opposite direction to the noise and could therefore have significantly attenuated it. - The sighting was made on the evening of February 4th, while the press published an article on the same day about a UFO in the sky relating to the February 2nd sighting. It is therefore possible that the witnesses of February 4th were on high alert and perceived something unusual in an observation that would have remained more commonplace without the initial sighting and its media coverage. GEIPAN classifies this case as B: Probable sighting of an aircraft.

summary: observation of a green ball in the sky
description: On February 1, 1985, around 6:00 PM, several witnesses observed a peculiar glow lasting for three seconds. Passing very quickly overhead, they saw a green sphere followed by a conical stream of light, ranging from pale yellow to bright red. This striking phenomenon remained silent. Although several factors suggested atmospheric reentry, no further information could be gathered about this event.

summary: Long observation of the slow ON passage of a luminous phenomenon: astronomical misinterpretation with Venus.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. Its publications include older cases, originally classified as type C, which are now being re-examined solely to improve the relevance of the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired over the past few years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification in an investigation report. This particular observation is classified as type C by SEPRA (Service for the Study of Atmospheric Re-entry Phenomena). On February 22, 1985, at approximately 7:40 PM, several witnesses observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon in the clear, starry sky to the west. The phenomenon was described as a green core from which green arrows emanated. Red lights also flashed regularly from the core. The ON movement of the luminous phenomenon was slow, and the observation lasted approximately one hour. Following a call for witnesses published in the local press, a witness to a similar observation that had taken place on January 31, 1985, came forward. This case was consistent (four witnesses, only two of whom could be interviewed), and the description of the observed UAP was precise. The sincerity and credibility of the witnesses were never questioned. The described phenomenon shared many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color, trajectory) with a well-known astronomical object: the planet Venus. Furthermore, Venus was indeed present in the observed area of the sky, even though the witness did not mention it, and was particularly bright. In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of weak strangeness is classified as UAP A, an observation linked to a misidentification of Venus.

summary: Probable observation of a distress flare
description: On January 26, 1986, five witnesses from different locations saw a red fireball. This very bright phenomenon moved, producing a thick plume of smoke. The police investigation determined that it was probably a distress flare fired by a local resident for testing.

summary: Initial observations of two flashes, then of the movement of an oval object surrounded by a halo: very probable observations of a meteoroid reentry.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named SAINT-GERMAIN (46) 1985, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On the night of January 24, 1985, two witnesses were startled by two successive flashes of light followed by clicking sounds and a sudden, intense, and brief flash of brightness. Above their house, these witnesses saw an object the shape and size of a rugby ball. This milky-white object then moved slowly and silently, surrounded by a whitish halo. Approximately three minutes later, these witnesses and others heard explosions. No power outages were observed in the house. The description includes the key characteristics of certain meteor reentry phenomena: - A bright light in the night, illuminating a large area. - An elongated, oval glow with a halo, crossing the sky. - Detonations occurring afterward. - Multiple witnesses over a potentially wide area. The police report collected testimonies from people living in the same house or neighboring areas. However, the appeal for witnesses by the local press (T1) led to the registration of about ten people in neighboring districts claiming to have made similar observations at the same time (no testimonies were recorded by the police). The various aspects of the phenomenon are delayed. The light in the night sky, which illuminates the area extensively, is caused by the meteorite at one or more specific moments (here, flashes followed by a longer period of illumination) during its entry into the atmosphere. This period of extreme brightness can be more or less prolonged; the meteorite may not have been within the field of vision of the witnesses, or they may not have had time to detect its initial focus in the sky. When it entered the witness's field of vision, its brightness had decreased (T1 said, "The day seemed very long, but it only lasted a few seconds; immediately afterward, night returned very quickly. At that moment, I saw an object or a white fireball arrive..."). The detonations can occur with a delay of varying lengths relative to the luminous phenomena. Indeed, these re-entry phenomena occur at high altitudes, between 100 and 20 km, and the sound propagation time (e.g., 330 m/s) to the ground can create delays of several minutes. It is also common for witnesses to perceive the phenomenon as being very close in the sky. GEIPAN has handled a significant number of cases over the last fifteen years, and nowadays, many sites record the data collected on the ground (by automatic cameras and/or through eyewitness accounts) during these re-entries. The characteristics These phenomena are now well known to GEIPAN, both in terms of their repeatability and variability, and the reports received are resolved without specific investigation. It is also becoming easier to re-examine older cases like this one, except when the reports are too brief and could leave room for doubt. An example from 2016 with more than 20 recordings on the website (International Meteor Organization) illustrates the operation of one of these sites, as well as the geographical spacing and the number of witnesses who could observe such a phenomenon. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as A: highly probable observation of a meteoroid reentry.

summary: observation of a bright point
description: On January 24, 1985, a motorist and his wife spotted a white dot with blue-green reflections. This dot, much larger than a star, followed a straight trajectory and left no trace or trail behind it. The observation lasted approximately 5 seconds before the object disappeared. No further information could be gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Strange luminous phenomenon observed inside a car.
description: On the evening of January 21, 1985, between 11:30 p.m. and midnight, witnesses saw flashes of light coming from a ruined house near their home. The investigation quickly revealed that it was caused by a short circuit in an electrical fence. Later that same evening, between 8:45 p.m. and 9:15 p.m., in the same area, a motorist and his wife witnessed a yellow, triangular light phenomenon that seemed to follow them for a moment before suddenly disappearing. None of the police units stationed in the area observed the phenomenon, and no further information could be gathered.

summary: Observation of about ten bright points in the sky.
description: On January 6, 1985, at approximately 11:00 PM, a witness observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon. About ten points of different colors—blue, yellow, or white—appeared above the city in several locations. They gradually disappeared behind clouds. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Observations on two different dates of luminous colored phenomena in the night sky: mistaken for the setting sun and for Mars at sunset.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named MORMOIRON (84) 1985, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On January 14, 1985, two witnesses, T1 and T2, observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon: a sphere approximately 3 meters in diameter whose color gradually changed from white to orange. This sphere, which became blinding, moved slowly and silently. It appeared to follow the vehicle before disappearing. Another witness, T3, had previously observed a glow on January 2nd, which did not move. After a police investigation and transmission to GEIPAN (the French UFO research group), the two observations remained linked as a single event without explanation, leading to a classification as category D. Re-examination of the case led to an explanation for each observation (see investigation notes). This re-examination resulted in the distinction of two separate phenomena: - UFO ne1: observed by T1 and T2 on January 14, 1985, after 5:15 PM. - UFO ne2: observed by T3 on January 2, 1985, after 9:00 PM. UAP No. 1 of January 14th: The description of the UAP's appearance on January 14th is consistent with the appearance of the sun near sunset (orange color) seen through a cloud layer: the UAP is indeed a smooth sphere, producing a dazzling light at times. The UAP's position and evolution also correspond. The presence of the sun near sunset in the direction of observation of the UAP is verified. The witnesses' perception of the UAP's movement is perfectly explained by the witnesses' own movement. This is a classic illusion known to GEIPAN (French Group for the Study of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena) that contributes to the strangeness and non-recognition of a celestial object by moving witnesses, an illusion known as the "following ball" illusion. The direction of the celestial object is, of course, absolutely fixed. When the car follows a roughly constant heading, the celestial object is fixed relative to the vehicle and moves with the landscape. Since the witness had already been surprised by the appearance of the UFO and perceived it to be at a close distance (hundreds of meters in this case), this movement along the landscape was understood as the UFO moving parallel to the vehicle, mirroring its speed. However, when the vehicle makes zigzags, the perception of parallel movement no longer holds true and is replaced by the perception of the UFO cutting straight across. The starting point of this misinterpretation, known as the "following sphere" phenomenon, seems to be the failure to recognize the sun when the witnesses are stationary. This is due to cloud cover obscuring and veiling the sun, creating rapidly changing appearances, light intensities, and colors (the witnesses noted the rapid movement of the clouds), as well as more or less total disappearances and reappearances. The variation in light intensity is typically interpreted by a witness who does not recognize the UFO as a change in distance, which is also a source of confusion. We also know that the sun behind scattered clouds can create beams of light, another obvious source of strangeness for those who don't recognize the sun. The perfect consistency between the true position of the sun and that of the UFO, and the "following ball" effect, leave little doubt about the explanation. Only the impossibility of stating that the sky was clear enough that evening for the sun to be visible to the witnesses prevents us from considering this hypothesis as certain. It is, however, highly probable. It can be noted that the witnesses were not familiar with the area, which may also have facilitated this misinterpretation. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as A: Misinterpretation of the sunset sun. UFO #2 of January 2, 1985: The description of the UFO's appearance as a pale orange color is consistent with the appearance of Mars. We verified that the position and evolution of the UFO also corresponded perfectly to those of Mars (within a few degrees). The observation should not have been very strange for the witness, and may have become more so when, 12 days later, he learned of the other observation (January 14th), reported in much stranger terms (and moreover by military personnel), with which a connection could be made. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as A: Mistaken identity with Mars at sunset.
